items.title: Muse Code + Spark 1.2 (Free Tier): Okay, this is ACTUALLY GOOD!
items.summary:
Visit TestSprite: https://www.testsprite.com/?via=aicodingki-dw
TestSprite CLI (Github Repo): https://github.com/TestSprite/testsprite-cli

In this video, I'll be testing Meta's new Muse Spark 1.2 model and its brand-new terminal coding agent, Muse Code. We'll look at the new coding upgrades, pricing, Muse Code features, and then run Muse Spark 1.2 through KingBench 3 to see how well it performs against models like Fable 5, Qwen 3.8 Max, Opus 4.8, Opus 5, Kimi K3, and more.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Meta has released Muse Spark 1.2, a coding-focused upgrade to Muse Spark 1.1.
💻 Muse Code is Meta’s new terminal coding agent, designed to work closely with Muse Spark 1.2.
🧠 The model has been trained heavily on long-horizon coding tasks, full repositories, and end-to-end projects.
⚙️ Muse Code includes async background agents, restart-safe runs, event logs, and useful slash commands.
💸 The pricing includes a cheaper data-sharing tier, plus $20 of free starting credit.
📊 Muse Spark 1.2 scored

items.transcript: [music] Hi, welcome to another video. So, Meta has just released Muse Spark 1.2 and along with it, they've also launched a brand new terminal coding agent called Muse Code. Muse Spark 1.2 2 is basically a coding focused update to Muse Spark 1.1 and Meta says it comes with improvements in code generation, complex debugging, codebase understanding, and end-to-end developer workflows. They've scaled up the training compute on coding tasks quite a lot this time, and they've also trained it extensively on long horizon coding tasks. Think whole repository generation, large end-to-end projects, and auto research style tasks. They're also doing this self-improvement loop thing where the model generates challenging coding environments for its own training, which is quite interesting. Now, the bigger part of this launch, if you ask me, is Musecode. It's their new terminal coding agent, kind of like their answer to Claude Code. It's in beta right now, and it's available on Mac OS and Linux via a simple command line install. The interesting bit here is that Muse Spark 1.2 has been co-rained with Musecode. So, the model and the harness are optimized to work together as one combo, and Meta says you'll get the best performance when you pair them up. The harness itself has some genuinely interesting design choices. Instead of spawning sub agents for individual tasks, it uses async background agents that stay active throughout your session. It also keeps a local event log that makes runs, replay exact, and restart safe. So, if your terminal dies mid task, you can just pick up right where it left off. It also comes with some bundled skills. There's slash plan, which gives you approval gated planning, so it won't just run off and do things without you signing off. Then there's /grill, which is my favorite one, where it basically stress tests its own plan and tries to poke holes in it before executing. And there's /goal for driving a task to completion. On the benchmark side, Meta is showing numbers on terminal bench 2.1, deepw 1.1, and their own internal coding bench. They also have this kernel optimization case study where muse spark 1.2 2 optimized GPU kernels over more than a thousand tool calls running for up to 24 hours and it beat the baseline implementations on both the KDA and MLA kernels. That's a nice flex, but as always take the company benchmarks with a grain of salt. We'll do our own testing in a bit. Now, let's talk about the pricing because this one is a bit different. There are two types of pricing here. There's the standard pricing and then there's a data sharing tier where if you allow them to train on your data, the price drops massively and it becomes really cheap. Personally, I think if you're already sharing your data with them, it would have been better if they just made it free in that mode. But they do give you $20 of free credit to start with. And considering how cheap the data sharing tier is, you can definitely stretch that credit for quite a long time. So, that's not bad at all. Now, let's test Muse Spark 1.2 on my own benchmark, Kingbench 3. Before we dive in, let me tell you something. Boris Churnney built Claude code and he said something that stuck with me. He doesn't write the prompts anymore. The loop does. His job is to write the loop. A loop acts, observes a real signal, decides what to do next, and repeats until a goal actually holds. Five blocks, trigger, goal, the work, memory, and verification. The feedback gate, the one block allowed to say, "No, not done yet." Everyone tunes the model and the prompt. Almost nobody builds this block. And in 2026, your loop is only as good as its feedback gate. Here's what that cost me. I had a loop running for 2 days. Test screen every single iteration. I came back to it proud of myself. Open the app and the whole checkout flow was dead button. Did nothing. No error. Just dead. The agent had been running unit tests against its own mocks the entire time. Green on its own machine. Reporting done on something no real user could actually use. A green run on the agent's own machine proves nothing. So the question I got stuck on is what's the one signal that actually closes the loop? And it's the boring answer. The deployed thing behaving for a real user. That's the block I tell you to obsess over. The verifier I use is open source, the test sprite CLI. The agent calls it midbuild and it drives the live app like a real user would, not Mox. The actual deployed thing. When it broke that checkout flow again, it didn't just say failed. It handed back a screenshot of exactly what the user would have seen. The dead button frozen. The agent read that patched it, reran. I wasn't in the loop for any of it. That's what a closed loop actually feels like. Not a bigger brain, a stricter referee. The model isn't your bottleneck anymore. The loop is, and the loop is only as good as what's allowed to tell it no. If you want to start using it, then the installation process is very simple. You'll need node 20.19, 22.13, or 24 and up. Install with npm install g at testbrite/estbrite cli. Grab your API key from the dashboard under settings API keys. Copy it. It only shows once. Run test setup. Paste your key in. Then confirm everything's connected with test sprite o status. That's it. You're ready to go. So when you design your next one, don't start with the model. Start with the verifier. For me, that's test sprite open- source Apache 2.0. Links below. It's a set of eight questions covering front-end 3D SVG generation maths and full endto-end agentic tasks. Each question is scored out of 10. So the maximum score is 80. I've already run this on a whole bunch of models so we can see exactly where it lands. The first question is the elevator simulation. Three elevators, people spawning on different floors, one person per elevator, proper queuing when someone gets left behind, tool tips on hover, all in one HTML file. Let's send it and see. Okay, the simulation works, but the queuing logic is a bit off and the animations are not that clean. It gets a five on this one. For comparison, Fable 5 got a nine here and Opus 5 both got full marks. So, not a great start. The second question is the 3JS contact lens case. It should have pronounced L and R caps, and you should be able to click the caps to open them up. Let's check. The case looks decent. The caps are there, and they're clickable, but the opening animation is a bit janky. I'll give it a seven. Fable 5 got a perfect 10 on this one. So, there's still a gap at the top. The third question is the 3JS folding table where a slider should smoothly fold and unfold the table in 3D. Let's send it. And this one is actually quite nice. The fold is seamless and it looks properly 3D. It gets an eight, which matches GLM 5.2 for one of the better scores on this test. The fourth question is the SVG of a panda eating a burger. Let's see. Okay. Wow. This is actually the best panda I've gotten in this entire benchmark. Clean shapes, proper burger. It actually looks like a panda eating a burger. Full 10 on this one. And believe it or not, that's the highest score of any model on this question. Chef's kiss. The fifth question is the bow and arrow simulator game with four targets and a timebased leaderboard. Let's send it and check. The game runs, but the aiming feels off and the leaderboard logic is halfbaked. It gets a five. Grock 4.5. Quen 3 08 mate max opus 48 and opus 5 all got full marks here. So this is a clear miss. The sixth question is the hard maths one. It's a permutation counting problem over ordered pairs and the answer should be 2460. Let's send it. And it gets exactly 2460 full 10. Most of the frontier models get this now but it's still good to see. The seventh question is the full agentic test. generate a data set of facts about pandas, finetune a Gemma 2B model on it, and give me a local web UI that serves a panda fact on every refresh all on its own. Let's wait a bit because this one takes a while and it's now done. The data set was generated, the Finetune ran locally, and the web UI works. Full 10 on this one, which is quite great to see, and it matches the best models on this test. The eighth and final question is the 3D wristwatch. A full-on wristwatch with smooth second, minute, and hour hands based on the current time, plus a date option and dual time zone tracking. This question absolutely destroys most models. Let's send it. And it actually produces a working 3D watch with smooth hands. The dual time zone part is a bit rough, but it gets a six, which is tied with DSV4 flash for the best score anyone has gotten on this question. Most models score 0 to3 here. So, this is impressive. So, this is the final chart and Muse Spark 1.2 2 lands at 61 out of 80, which is 76.25%. That puts it in fifth place on the leaderboard, just behind Kimmy K3 and Opus 5 at 77.5%. Opus 4.8 at 80%. Quen 3.8 Max at 81.25%. And Fable 5 at the top with 82.5%. Now, here's the thing. Muspark 1.1 scored 60% on this exact same benchmark. So, this is a jump of over 16 points in one point release, which is a really good jump. Meta is closing the gap with the Frontier much faster than I expected. As for my overall thoughts after using it, the model is good. The front-end work is where it really shines. The SVG test, the folding table, and the watch test show that it has genuinely strong visual and front-end capabilities, arguably some of the best out there right now, but it does suck a bit at back end and the more complex, longer tasks. You can see it in the elevator simulation and the game test where the logic side of things falls apart. I hope that gets fixed soon because the front end side is already there. It's also still prone to overwriting files and not understanding instructions well, which is kind of wonky in real life usage. It'll sometimes rewrite an entire file when you asked for a small change, and that gets annoying fast when you're working in a real codebase, even with the Muse code harness doing its restart safe magic. On the whole, though, this is a solid release. The pricing with the data sharing tier is really aggressive. The $20 free credit is a nice touch. The harness has some genuinely fresh ideas with the async agents and the event log and the model itself made a big leap on my benchmark. Now, the one thing I'm still hoping for is that they also launch an open model soon. Meta used to be the open weights champion and it would be great to see a Muse Spark open release that the community can actually build on. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button.
